newsitem.title: UK: British parties clash on unions, law and order.
newsitem.headline: British parties clash on unions, law and order.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives on Saturday accused the Labour Party of reaching a secret deal with the trade unions ahead of the May 1 election.

Labour, moving in on a policy area the Conservatives have long regarded as their own, pledged tough new measures on law and order and a crackdown on the drunken violence the party says has turned many city centres into no-go areas for families.
Conservative Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said impending walkouts by firefighters in Essex, eastern England, were evidence that Labour would give the unions a "licence to strike".
"They are going to give them the right to strike without the fear of the sack." Heseltine told an election campaign news conference.

Denouncing Labour's Tony Blair as "Phoney Tony", a favourite Conservative taunt, Heseltine said that while the Labour leader had called in public for a fair deal for the unions, "you offered a secret deal in private".

The ruling party, trailing by a massive 20 points in opinion polls, is keen to raise the spectre of unfettered trades union power, a major factor in Labour's 1979 election defeat which ushered in 18 years of Conservative power.
The Conservatives say that Blair, as part of his moves to shift Labour towards the centre ground, has persuaded the unions to remain in the background until after the election.
"The atmosphere is changing as the unions get used to the idea that it might be back to the old days," said Heseltine.

Labour, however, accused the Conservatives of trying to score political points over the Essex firefighters' dispute, in which the Fire Brigades Union has voted to hold two 24-hour strikes later this month in protest at budget cuts.
"The Tories (Conservatives) are trying to exploit these matters for their political interest rather than trying to find agreement," Labour deputy leader John Prescott told BBC radio.
Labour's home affairs spokesman Jack Straw distanced his party from the firefighters' strike, saying the dispute should be settled by arbitration.
"We don't believe the strike is justified," he told a campaign news conference.

Straw, who has taken as tough a line on crime as any Conservative Home Secretary, said the party would introduce new measures against the drunken violence that caused many people to avoid town centres at weekends for fear of being attacked.
"Labour will call time on drunken thugs," Straw said.

A key measure would be the wider use of toughened-glass beer mugs, which would shatter into tiny pieces when smashed, rather than break into splinters which could inflict horrific injuries if used in bar-room brawls.

The Conservatives also used their regular campaign news conference to stress their credentials on defence, an area where they always scored over the old, pre-Blair Labour Party which was once wedded to unilateral nuclear disarmament.

Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said Labour needed to cover a "black hole" in its spending plans and this meant that "both the defence of this country and jobs in the defence industry are at risk".
But Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown said Blair had made clear that a defence review would be led by security considerations.
